title: Browsers
subtitle: Your browser and search engine are the two main sources of data collection during everyday internet use. Switching away from Chrome is one of the highest-impact changes you can make.

context.title: What's actually being collected
context.body: Every search you make on Google is stored, timestamped, and tied to your account or IP address. Chrome sends browsing data back to Google by default, including URLs you visit and keystrokes in the address bar. Your ISP also logs every DNS request your browser makes - essentially a record of every site you've visited.
context.body2: Switching browsers and search engines doesn't require technical skill. For most people, Firefox with DuckDuckGo is a straightforward drop-in replacement that eliminates the majority of this surveillance.

warning.body: Chrome disabled the full version of uBlock Origin with the Manifest V3 rollout. If you're still using Chrome, you've lost an effective ad and tracker blocker. This alone is a good reason to switch browsers.

items.name: Switch away from Chrome
items.why: Chrome is Google's primary data collection tool for the web. It sends browsing behavior back to Google servers, syncs your history across devices tied to your Google account, and now limits effective ad blocking via Manifest V3. Every Chrome user is, to some degree, a data product.

steps.text: Download Firefox at `mozilla.org/firefox` or Brave at `brave.com`
During setup, import your bookmarks and saved passwords from Chrome: `Menu → Bookmarks → Import bookmarks and settings`
Set your new browser as the system default: on Mac `System Settings → Desktop & Dock → Default web browser`, on Windows `Settings → Apps → Default apps`
On mobile, set it as default in `iPhone Settings → [Browser name] → Default Browser App` or `Android Settings → Apps → Default apps → Browser`

items.name: Tighten Firefox privacy settings
items.why: Firefox's default privacy mode is good but not maxed out. A few minutes in settings significantly reduces what Firefox and third parties can collect from your browsing sessions, and turns off Mozilla's own telemetry.

steps.text: Open `Settings` → `Privacy & Security`. Set Enhanced Tracking Protection to `Strict`
Under Cookies and Site Data, enable `Delete cookies and site data when Firefox is closed`
Under History, set Firefox to `Never remember history` or use custom settings to clear history on close
Scroll to Firefox Data Collection and Use - uncheck all boxes to disable sending telemetry to Mozilla
Under Address Bar - Firefox Suggest, disable `Contextual suggestions` and `Suggestions from the web` to stop keystrokes being sent to Mozilla
For Brave users: defaults are already strict - go to `Settings → Shields` and set trackers and ads blocking to `Aggressive`

items.name: Replace Google with a private search engine
items.why: Google stores every search you make and links it to your account or a persistent identifier. Over time this creates an extraordinarily detailed picture of your interests, health concerns, finances, relationships, and beliefs. Private search engines don't store or sell this data.

steps.text: In Firefox: `Settings` → `Search` → `Default Search Engine` → select DuckDuckGo or add a custom engine
In Brave: `Settings` → `Search engine` → choose Brave Search or DuckDuckGo
On iPhone Safari: `Settings` → `Apps` → `Safari` → `Search Engine` → DuckDuckGo
Best options: `DuckDuckGo` (no tracking), `Startpage` (Google results without tracking), `Brave Search` (independent index), `Kagi` (paid, best quality)

items.name: Enable third-party cookie blocking
items.why: When you visit a website, it may load invisible elements from third-party ad networks that set cookies in your browser. Those cookies follow you across every other site that loads the same ad network - building a detailed map of your browsing activity even on sites you've never visited directly.

steps.text: Firefox with Strict Enhanced Tracking Protection (configured above) blocks third-party cookies automatically
Brave blocks third-party cookies by default - verify at `Settings → Privacy and security → Block third-party cookies`
On Safari (iPhone/Mac): `Settings → Safari → Privacy & Security` → ensure `Prevent Cross-Site Tracking` is enabled
If you must use Chrome: `Settings → Privacy and security → Cookies → Block third-party cookies`

items.name: Install recommended privacy extensions
items.why: Extensions can both protect and compromise your privacy. A malicious or poorly maintained extension has full access to every page you visit and everything you type - including passwords. Stick to well-known, open-source extensions with large user bases.

steps.text: `uBlock Origin` - blocks ads, trackers, and malicious scripts. The single most impactful extension for privacy. Firefox and Brave only - not available in full form on Chrome
`ClearURLs` - strips tracking parameters from URLs before they load, preventing click-through tracking
`Privacy Badger` (by EFF) - learns to block third-party trackers based on behavior. Good complement to uBlock Origin
After installing uBlock Origin, open its dashboard and enable the `EasyPrivacy` and `uBlock filters - Privacy` filter lists
Resist installing more extensions than you need - each one adds to your browser fingerprint

items.name: Always reject non-essential cookies
items.path: Applies on every website you visit
items.why: When you click 'Accept all cookies,' you're explicitly consenting to being tracked by that site and often dozens of third-party ad networks. 'Necessary cookies only' limits the site to cookies required for the page to function - no tracking, no advertising profiles.

steps.text: When a cookie banner appears, look for `Reject all`, `Necessary only`, or `Manage preferences` - never click `Accept all`
If there's no obvious reject option, click `Manage preferences` and manually disable all non-essential categories (marketing, analytics, personalization)
For automatic cookie rejection, uBlock Origin's Annoyances filter list can auto-dismiss many cookie banners - enable it in the uBlock Origin dashboard under filter lists

items.name: Secure your home router
items.why: Your router's default admin password is often printed on the device itself or is a known default - making it trivially easy for anyone on your network to access router settings. Your router's default name (SSID) often includes the make and model, which can reveal known vulnerabilities to nearby attackers.

steps.text: Log into your router admin panel - the address is usually printed on the router label. Common defaults: `192.168.1.1` or `192.168.0.1`
Change the default admin username and password to something strong and unique. Store it in your password manager
Change the Wi-Fi network name (SSID) to something that doesn't reveal your router's make, model, or your name
Verify your router encryption is set to `WPA3` or at minimum `WPA2` - avoid WEP. Disable `WPS` if you don't use it (it has known vulnerabilities)
Check for and apply any available firmware updates for your router

items.name: Understanding when a VPN helps (and when it doesn't)
items.path: Applies if you choose to use a VPN
items.why: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, masking your IP address from sites you visit and preventing your ISP from seeing which sites you visit. It shifts trust from your ISP to your VPN provider. However, a VPN does not make you anonymous - if you're logged into Google while using a VPN, Google still knows who you are.

steps.text: A VPN is most useful on public Wi-Fi (airports, cafes) where your traffic is otherwise visible to the network operator
Choose a provider with a verified no-logs policy confirmed by an independent third-party audit
Never use a free VPN (except Proton VPN's free tier) - free VPNs monetize by selling your data
Reputable audited options: `Proton VPN`, `Mullvad`, `NordVPN`, `Surfshark`, `ExpressVPN`, `Private Internet Access`

items.name: Understand and reduce browser fingerprinting
items.why: Websites can identify you by combining your screen resolution, installed fonts, GPU, timezone, language settings, and more. This fingerprint is often unique enough to track you across sites without any tracking cookies. Adding many browser extensions makes your fingerprint more unique and easier to identify.

steps.text: Use Brave - it randomizes your fingerprint on each site visit, making it harder to link your sessions across sites
Firefox with uBlock Origin also significantly reduces fingerprinting surface
Keep your extension count low - each extension changes your browser's fingerprint
Test your current fingerprint at `coveryourtracks.eff.org` - a tool from the EFF that shows how unique your browser appears to trackers
For maximum fingerprint resistance, use Tor Browser - it makes all users look identical by design
